rows.grounds: describes the initial state and method of one who does not know the jewel's truth
locates the attainment of the meansless non-conceptual state
names the one who knows the jewel

items.question: How does one become a knower of the jewel?
premises: One may first not know the truth of the jewel.
Such a person practices through the means of certainty.
This leads to attaining the meansless non-conceptual state.
items.inference: Through certainty-based practice one reaches the meansless state and is called a knower of the jewel.
uncertainties: The exact referent of ratna as jewel or essence is context-dependent.
items.plain_english: One who does not know the truth of the jewel may first practice through the means of certainty; by attaining the meansless, non-conceptual state, that person is called a knower of the jewel.

rows.grounds: identifies the means of non-difference stated here
describes the means whose nature is both difference and non-difference

items.question: How are the three means classified in this teaching?
premises: The means of non-difference is stated here as śāmbhava.
The means whose nature is both difference and non-difference is called śākta.
The means of difference is called āṇava.
items.inference: The three means are classified as śāmbhava, śākta, and āṇava according to non-difference, mixed, and difference.
items.plain_english: Here the means of non-difference is called śāmbhava, the means of both difference and non-difference is called śākta, and the means of difference is called āṇava.

rows.grounds: specifies the knowledge in this context
qualifies knowledge as accompanied by means
names the full range of ritual action
states that action will be contained within knowledge

items.question: What happens to ritual action within knowledge accompanied by means?
premises: Knowledge here is accompanied by means.
The entire expanse of action exists.
Action can appear in a very clear form.
items.inference: In the culmination of knowledge with means, the whole expanse of action will be included within it in a clear form.
items.plain_english: In the end, within knowledge accompanied by means, the entire expanse of action will be included in a very clear form.

rows.grounds: denies that action is a thing other than knowledge
gives the reason for assuming sequential form
states that sequential form is assumed

items.question: What is the true nature of action in relation to knowledge?
premises: Action is not a thing other than knowledge.
Knowledge can assume a sequential nature through the force of means.
This sequential form has been previously identified as action.
items.inference: Action is knowledge itself appearing in sequential form due to the operation of means.
items.plain_english: Action is not something other than knowledge; it is knowledge that has taken on a sequential form through the force of means, and this was stated earlier as action.

rows.grounds: identifies right knowledge as the sole cause of liberation
names the divisions of self, other, and so forth

items.question: Why is right knowledge the sole cause of liberation?
premises: Right knowledge abides in both self and other.
The divisions of self, other, and so on are mere constructions.
Liberation depends on seeing through such constructed divisions.
items.inference: Because the divisions of self and other are mere constructions, right knowledge that abides in both is the sole cause of liberation.
items.plain_english: Right knowledge, abiding in both self and other, is the sole cause of liberation, because the divisions of self, other, and so on are nothing more than constructions.

rows.grounds: describes the teacher as having the nature of unity's flashing forth
describes the teacher as one in nature

items.question: When is a teacher called accomplished and liberated?
premises: All appearances may be equally constructed.
A teacher may embody the flashing forth of unity.
Such unity makes the teacher one in nature.
items.inference: When a teacher embodies the flashing forth of unity amid equally constructed appearances, that teacher is called accomplished and liberated.
items.plain_english: Even when all things are equally constructed, a teacher whose nature is the flashing forth of unity is called one-natured, accomplished, and liberated.

rows.grounds: sets the extent of the teacher's continuum
identifies the continuum as the teacher
describes the continuum as made of right knowledge
indicates liberation by one's own self

items.question: How far does the teacher's liberating presence extend?
premises: The teacher is identified with the extent of that continuum.
That continuum is made of right knowledge.
Right knowledge brings liberation by one's own self.
items.inference: Because the teacher's continuum is made of right knowledge, one is liberated by one's own self through it.
items.plain_english: As far as that continuum extends, it is declared to be the teacher; and because it is made of right knowledge, one is liberated by one's own self through it.

rows.grounds: states that the knower carries the continuum across

items.question: Why can the knower carry the continuum across to liberation?
premises: The knower is established as one with that continuum.
This unity is supported by reason and scripture.
Right knowledge operates across that continuum.
items.inference: Because the sage is one with that continuum, the knower carries the continuum across, as established by reason and scripture.
items.plain_english: For that very reason the knower carries his own continuum across; this is well established by reason and scripture, because to that extent the sage is one.

rows.grounds: introduces an objection in this context
states that they raise an objection
states the claim that liberation comes from knowledge

items.question: How can ritual action lead to liberation if knowledge alone liberates?
premises: Liberation is said to come from knowledge.
Initiation and related rites are forms of action.
An objection asks how action could bring liberation.
items.inference: The verse presents the objection that ritual action seems incompatible with liberation through knowledge alone.
items.plain_english: Therefore some object here: if liberation comes from knowledge, how could initiation and other ritual actions bring about liberation?

rows.grounds: proposes that action is of the nature of knowledge
refers to the one in whom knowledge is situated
states the expected effect of knowledge
raises the case of another person

items.question: How is the objection about knowledge and another's liberation answered?
premises: The objection claims knowledge should liberate only where it is located.
It also questions how another could be liberated.
The text says these objectors are dismissed at the root.
items.inference: The objection is rejected as baseless, and the verse turns to what others have established instead.
uncertainties: The exact force of the concessive reply in the middle of the verse is compressed.
items.plain_english: If action is of the nature of knowledge, the objectors ask whether knowledge liberates only where it is located and what happens in liberating another; but they are dismissed at the root, and the text turns to what others have established.

rows.grounds: gives an analogy for the removing action

items.question: What alternative view explains impurity and initiation as substances and acts?
premises: Some hold that impurity is a substance.
They compare it to a film on the eye.
They compare initiation to acts like applying collyrium.
items.inference: The verse presents the view that initiation is a ritual action that removes a substantial impurity, like medicine removing an eye defect.
items.plain_english: Some say impurity is a substance, like a film over the eye, and initiation is the action that removes it, like applying collyrium.

rows.grounds: characterizes the view as rejected by reason and scripture
refers to the real status of the bonds

items.question: How will the text treat the substantialist view of impurity and the bonds?
premises: The previous verse presented a substantialist view of impurity.
That view is said to be condemned by reason and scripture.
The status of impurity, māyā, and karma still needs explanation.
items.inference: The text will refute the substantialist view and later explain the true status of impurity, māyā, and karma.
items.plain_english: We will refute that view later, since it is condemned by reason and scripture, and we will also show the true status of impurity, māyā, and karma.

rows.grounds: describes knowledge as operating through the three powers
locates the classification within that knowledge
names the lowest or last level
identifies the last as the root
orders the middle, higher, and first levels

items.question: How are the levels of knowledge ordered within the three-power means?
premises: Knowledge operates through the means of the three powers.
That knowledge has multiple levels.
The levels can be ordered from root to highest.
items.inference: Within knowledge operating through the three powers, the last is the root, above it the middle, and above that the highest first level.
uncertainties: The compressed compound describing the upper levels allows slight variation in unpacking.
items.plain_english: Thus, in the knowledge that operates through the means of the three powers, the last is the root, above it is the middle, and above that is the highest, first level.

rows.grounds: points to a level beyond the previous ones
names this knowledge as unsurpassed and resting in the power of bliss

items.question: What knowledge lies beyond the means-based levels?
premises: The previous verse described levels within means-based knowledge.
There is a knowledge beyond those levels.
That knowledge rests in the power of bliss and is unsurpassed.
items.inference: Beyond the means-based levels is a supreme, unsurpassed knowledge free of means and resting in the power of bliss.
items.plain_english: Even beyond that is a supreme knowledge, free of means and the rest, resting in the power of bliss; here it is called the unsurpassed.

rows.grounds: describes the supreme knowledge as self-luminous
names exalted beings for whom it is rare
states that its true presence is hard to attain

items.question: How rare is the self-luminous supreme knowledge according to scripture?
premises: The supreme knowledge is self-luminous.
Even exalted beings such as lords of knowledge find it rare.
The revered Siddha Tantra states this.
items.inference: Scripture declares that this self-luminous knowledge is rare even for exalted beings like the lords of knowledge.
uncertainties: The exact scope of vidyāvidyeśvarādibhiḥ may include related classes of beings.
items.plain_english: That self-luminous knowledge, whose true presence is rare even for the lords of knowledge and others, is spoken of in the revered Siddha Tantra.

rows.grounds: locates the indication in the eighteenth chapter
grounds the claim in a scriptural statement

items.question: Where else is this rare knowledge indicated in scripture?
premises: The Mālinī scripture discusses this knowledge.
The eighteenth chapter indicates it clearly.
A statement says it is not attained without Śaṅkara's grace.
items.inference: The Mālinī scripture clearly indicates that this knowledge depends on the grace of Śaṅkara.
items.plain_english: This is also clearly indicated in the Mālinī, in the eighteenth chapter, by the statement that it is not attained without the grace of Śaṅkara.

rows.grounds: describes its fruit as accomplishment and liberation
describes the composition of the treatise
identifies the work as a teaching

items.question: What is the author systematizing in the Tantrāloka based on this teaching?
premises: The Mālinīvijayottara presents a relevant teaching.
That teaching concerns a fourfold knowledge.
This fourfold knowledge brings accomplishment and liberation.
items.inference: The author systematizes the fourfold knowledge that yields accomplishment and liberation in the teaching called Tantrāloka.
items.plain_english: By this very teaching in the Mālinīvijayottara, the fourfold knowledge that brings the great rise of accomplishment and liberation is systematized by me in this teaching called the Tantrāloka.

rows.grounds: describes the object before its form is unfolded
states its initial mode of appearance

items.question: How does anything first appear in reflective awareness?
premises: Anything may be reflected on inwardly or outwardly.
Before its form is unfolded, it still appears.
This appearance is the first stage of apprehension.
items.inference: Whatever is reflected on, inwardly or outwardly, first shines forth with its form not yet unfolded.
items.plain_english: Here, whatever is reflected on, whether inwardly or outwardly, first shines forth with its form not yet unfolded.

rows.grounds: describes the initial appearance as unopened
identifies doubt as arising from that manifestation

items.question: Under what condition does doubt arise from an initial manifestation?
premises: The first manifestation appears with an unopened, indescribable form.
Doubt concerns some possible form.
Doubt does not arise without some determination.
items.inference: Doubt arises only when an initially unopened manifestation is present together with some determination about a form.
items.plain_english: That first manifestation appears with an unopened, indescribable form; doubt arises only when some form is determined, and not otherwise.

rows.grounds: expresses the questioning form of doubt
identifies a determined part within the primary appearance
states that part is clearly determined
describes doubt as having properties like existence and non-existence not yet unfolded

items.question: What is the structure of doubt expressed as 'what is this'?
premises: Doubt takes the form of asking what something is.
Within that appearance some part is already determined.
Properties such as existence or non-existence remain unopened.
items.inference: Doubt is a mixed state in which one part is determined while properties like existence or non-existence remain unopened.
items.plain_english: In the question 'what is this?', one part of the primary appearance is already well determined, while doubt remains because properties such as 'it is' or 'it is not' are not yet unfolded.

rows.grounds: takes the word 'what' as the subject
denies an extra meaning beyond the object
describes the object as not yet opened in form
states that the word denotes the thing itself in that state

items.question: What does the word 'what' actually signify in doubt?
premises: The word 'what' appears in expressions of doubt.
It does not add a separate meaning beyond the object.
It points to the object whose form is not yet opened.
items.inference: The word 'what' signifies the object itself in an unopened state rather than adding an extra meaning.
items.plain_english: The word 'what' does not reveal any additional meaning; it simply denotes the thing itself while its form remains unopened.

rows.grounds: denies that this is the primary doubt
locates the process among multiple properties

items.question: Why is 'post or person' not the primary form of doubt?
premises: The example 'post or person' presents explicit alternatives.
Primary doubt concerns an unopened object.
Determination arises among many possible properties.
items.inference: The 'post or person' case is not primary doubt but the arising of determination among multiple properties.
items.plain_english: The doubt 'is it a post or a person?' is not the primary kind of doubt; it is really the arising of determination among many possible properties.

rows.grounds: explains doubt from the non-unfolding of two reflectable forms
names the state again as doubt
states that the distinction is clear

items.question: How does doubt differ from conceptual construction in this analysis?
premises: Doubt arises when two reflectable forms remain unopened.
This occurs in the 'what' aspect of apprehension.
Conceptual construction operates differently.
items.inference: Doubt belongs to the unopened 'what' aspect, whereas conceptual construction is a different and clearer operation.
items.plain_english: Again, doubt arises in the 'what' aspect because two forms that could be reflected on remain unopened; conceptual construction, by contrast, is clearly different.

rows.grounds: identifies the first manifestation as that of an unopened nature
refers back to the first manifestation

items.question: What is the first manifestation called in this analysis of inquiry?
premises: The first manifestation presents being with an unopened nature.
This stage precedes clear determination.
The text identifies it with indication, question, and doubt.
items.inference: The first manifestation of an unopened nature is identified here as indication, question, and doubt.
items.plain_english: Therefore, the first manifestation of a being whose nature is not yet unfolded is here called indication, question, and indeed doubt.
